newsitem.title: PANAMA: FEATURE - Scientists seek to prevent drying of Panama Canal.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Scientists seek to prevent drying of Panama Canal.

text.p: Try imagining the Panama Canal without water. Scientists warn it could happen early in the next century because of silt and sediment accumulating in the waters surrounding the strategic waterway.

To keep such a scenario from becoming reality, a group of Panamanian and American scientists has embarked on a $1.5-million study to monitor sedimention in the Central American canal's 805,000-acre (330,000-hectare) watershed. Experts from Panama's National Institute for Natural Resources (INRENARE) and the U.S. Smithsonian Institute plan a meticulous study of sedimentation, deforestation and the loss of flora and fauna.

The two-year project funded by the U.S. Agency for International Development (AID) should provide canal and government officials with fresh data. "The new canal authority ... will then determine the amount of money needed to tackle the problem," Alexis Baules, an AID forestry expert working on the project, said, referring to the planned handover of the U.S.- administered canal to Panama on Dec. 31, 1999.

Baules said INRENARE experts first sought funds from AID nearly a decade ago after noticing population growth and highways encroaching in the canal's watershed. Part of Panama City's major highway, Simon Bolivar Avenue, runs through the watershed.
"After years of erosion caused by deforestation and overpopulation ... the canal could face problems in about 20 years due to sedimentation," he predicted.

The Panama Canal Commission (PCC) has already gathered sedimentation data from two studies conducted in the 1980s. But these concentrated on Madden Lake, one of the two major lakes feeding the canal, because it has steep slopes and is more susceptible to torrential downpours and erosion, Juan Hector Diaz, an environmental officer with the PCC, said.

Diaz stressed that the AID-funded study would be the first to measure sedimentation in the transoceanic canal's entire watershed, targeting both canal feeder lakes Madden and Gatun. "Population has increased in the canal watershed. The threat is there and every effort to protect it is welcome," he said. "Previous studies showed a fractional amount of sedimentation ... There is still time to protect the watershed."

Diaz said sedimentation was still normal and canal authorities foresaw no change in procedures to fight it. "Every channel in the world has erosion, it's a natural process. Right now, we don't plan to counteract the erosion because it's not a problem. But we will monitor it," he said.

In the U.S. AID study, scientists will take water samples to calculate the rate of sedimentation, Robert Stallard, a member of the U.S. Geological Service, said. They will use photographs to monitor the rate of deforestation, said Stallard, who is working on similar erosion projects in Puerto Rico, Venezuela and the Mississippi valley.

"We're also going to study the sociological component, who's doing the chopping of the trees and why," he told Reuters. "We can't solve the problem without looking at people and their need to survive".

Parts of the study will be modelled on a project Stallard is working on in San Juan, Puerto Rico, where he has been monitoring the slow destruction fo the city's water reserves. Deforestation and population growth caused sediment to slide into the reserves and destroy them, he said.
"In Puerto Rico, they're trying to fix the problem. But the reforestation projects are too late. It will take hundreds of years before sediments stop coming into the reserves."
